items.question: What do you find intellectually exciting about working in robotics?
items.object: Robotics as a field of research
items.answer: At the beginning, I was really excited about the impact that robotics could have in the world, but at the same time, I was also really fascinated by this problem of developing perception and intelligence in machines. Robots embody all of that, and also there's sometimes some cool math that you can do as well that keeps your brain active, makes you think. So I think all of that is really fun about working in the field.
quotes: At the beginning, I was really excited about the impact that robotics could have in the world, but at the same time, I was also really fascinated by this problem of developing perception and intelligence in machines. Robots embody all of that, and also there's sometimes some cool math that you can do as well that keeps your brain active, makes you think. So I think all of that is really fun about working in the field.

rubrics.text: The response presents robotics as a meeting point between real-world impact and the problem of developing perception and intelligence in machines.

items.question: What do you see as the central challenge in getting learned robot skills to work across different environments and objects?
items.object: Generalization in robot learning
items.answer: Since that beginning point, it was very clear to me that we could train robots to do pretty cool things, but getting the robot to do one of those things in many scenarios with many objects was a major challenge. Ten years ago, we were training robots to screw a cap onto a bottle, use a spatula to lift an object into a bowl, do a tight insertion, or hang a hanger on a clothes rack. Pretty cool stuff, but actually getting the robot to do that in many environments with many objects—that's where a big part of the challenge comes in. I've been thinking about ways to make broader data sets and train on those broader data sets, and also different approaches for learning, whether it be reinforcement learning, video prediction, imitation learning, all those things.
quotes: Since that beginning point, it was very clear to me that we could train robots to do pretty cool things, but getting the robot to do one of those things in many scenarios with many objects was a major challenge. rubrics.text: The response identifies generalizing an already learned robot skill across environments and objects as the bottleneck relative to demonstrating that skill in a specific setting.

items.question: Why are you pursuing a general-purpose model at Physical Intelligence?
items.object: Physical Intelligence's general-purpose approach to robotics
items.answer: We're trying to build a big neural network model that could ultimately control any robot to do anything in any scenario. A big part of our vision is that in the past, robotics has focused on trying to go deep on one application, developing a robot to do one thing, and then ultimately gotten kind of stuck in that one application. It's really hard to solve one thing and then try to get out of that and broaden. Instead, we're in it for the long term to try to address this broader problem with physical intelligence in the real world.
quotes: So we're trying to build a big neural network model that could ultimately control any robot to do anything in any scenario. Instead, we're in it for the long term to try to address this broader problem with physical intelligence in the real world.

rubrics.text: The response states that developing robotics around a single application makes it difficult to later broaden to other applications.

items.question: Why do you think using data across different robot platforms is important for building generalist robots?
items.object: Using data across different robot embodiments
items.answer: We're thinking a lot about generalization, generalists, and, unlike other robotics companies, we think that being able to leverage all of the possible data is very important. This comes down to not just leveraging data from one robot, but from any robot platform that might have six joints or seven joints or two arms or one arm. We've seen a lot of evidence that you could transfer a lot of rich information across these different embodiments. It allows you to use data, and if you iterate on your robot platform, you don't have to throw all your data away. We've had a lot of pain in the past where we got a new version of the robot and then your policy doesn't work, and it's a really painful process to try to get back to where you were on the previous robot iteration. So, trying to build generalist robots and essentially develop foundation models that will power the next generation of robots in the real world.

items.question: Why do you see collecting real-world robot data as central to Physical Intelligence's approach?
items.object: Scaling real-world robot data
items.answer: At the beginning, we were just getting off the ground. We were trying to scale data collection, and a big part of that is, unlike in language, we don't have Wikipedia or an internet of robot motions. We're really excited about scaling data on real robots in the real world. This kind of real data is what has fueled machine learning advances in the past, and a big part of that is we actually need to collect that data. That looks like teleoperating robots in the physical world. We're also exploring other ways of scaling data, but the bread and butter is scaling real robot data.

items.question: How do you assess the generalization demonstrated by Physical Intelligence's October robot release?
items.object: Generalization and language interaction in Physical Intelligence's October demonstration
items.answer: We released something in late October where we showed some of our initial efforts around scaling data and how we can learn very complex tasks of folding laundry, cleaning tables, and constructing a cardboard box. Where we are in that journey is really thinking a lot about language interaction and generalization to different environments. What we showed in October was the robot in one environment, and it had data in that environment. We were able to see some amount of generalization: it was able to fold shirts that it had never seen before, fold shorts that it had never seen before. But the degree of generalization was very limited, and you also couldn't interact with it in any way. You couldn't prompt it and tell it what you want it to do beyond fairly basic things that it saw in the training data. Being able to handle lots of different prompts and lots of different environments is a big focus right now.

items.question: Why do you find pre-trained vision-language models useful for building robot foundation models?
items.object: Pre-trained vision-language models for robot control
items.answer: In terms of the architecture, we're using Transformers, and we are using pre-trained models, pre-trained vision-language models, and that allows you to leverage all of the rich information on the internet. We had a research result a couple years ago where we showed that if you leverage vision-language models, you could actually get the robot to do tasks that require concepts that were never in the robot's training data but were on the internet. One famous example is that you can pass the cat can to Taylor Swift, or a picture of Taylor Swift, and the robot has never seen Taylor Swift in person, but the internet has lots of images of Taylor Swift in it. You can leverage all the information in that data and then the weights of the pre-trained model to transfer that to the robot, so we're not starting from scratch, and that helps a lot as well.

items.question: Why do you see more diverse robot data as the main priority for improving robots' generalizability?
items.object: Diversity of robot training data
items.answer: I think the number one thing, and this is kind of the boring thing, is just getting more diverse robot data. For that release we had in late October last year, we collected data in three buildings. The internet, for example, and everything that has fueled language models and vision models, is way more diverse than that, because the internet is pictures taken by lots of people and texts written by lots of different people. So just trying to collect data in many more diverse places, with many more objects and many more tasks—scaling the diversity of the data, not just the quantity of the data, is very important. That's a big thing we're focusing on right now: bringing our robots into lots of different places and collecting data in them. As a side product of that, we also learn what it takes to get your robot to be operational and functional in lots of different places, and that's a really nice byproduct because if you actually want to get robots to work in the real world, you need to be able to do that.

items.question: What kinds of reasoning do you see as useful for robots performing everyday tasks?
items.object: Basic reasoning in robotics
items.answer: We're also exploring other things: leveraging videos of people, data from the web, pre-trained models, and thinking about reasoning, although more basic forms of reasoning. For example, putting a dirty shirt into a hamper: if you can recognize where the shirt is and where the hamper is and what you need to do to accomplish that task, that's useful. Or if you want to make a sandwich and the user has a particular request in mind, you should reason through that request. If they're allergic to pickles, you probably shouldn't put pickles on the sandwich. Things like that. The number one thing is just more diverse robot data.

items.question: Why have you deliberately chosen to share Physical Intelligence's model weights, research, and robot designs openly?
items.object: Physical Intelligence's decision to openly share models, research, and robot designs
items.answer:
We've actually been quite open. Not only have we open-sourced some of the weights and released details in technical papers, we've also been working with hardware companies and giving designs of robots to hardware companies. Some people are really shocked when I tell them this: what about the IP, what about confidentiality and stuff like that? We've made a very intentional choice around this. There are a couple reasons for it. One is that we think the field is really just at the beginning, and these models will be so much better, and the robots should be so much better, in a year, in three years. We want to support the development of the research and the community, support the robots, so that when we hopefully develop the technology of these generalist models, the world will be more ready for it. We'll have more robust robots that are able to leverage those models, and people who have the expertise and understand what it requires to use those models.

The other thing is that we have a really fantastic team of researchers and engineers. Really fantastic researchers and engineers want to work at companies that are open, especially researchers, where they can get credit for their work, share their ideas, and talk about their ideas. We think that having the best researchers and engineers will be necessary for solving this problem.

The last thing I'll mention is that I think the biggest risk with this bet is that it won't work. I'm not really worried about competitors; I'm more worried that no one will solve the problem.

items.question: Why do you think robotics is such a hard problem to solve?
items.object: The difficulty of solving robotics
items.answer: I think robotics is very hard, and there have been many, many failures in the past. Unlike when you're recognizing an object in an image, there's very little tolerance for error. You can miss a grasp on an object, or the difference between making contact and not making contact with an object is so small, and it has a massive impact on whether your robot can successfully manipulate the object. That's just one example. There are challenges on the data side of collecting data.

items.question: How do you think about finding early applications for Physical Intelligence’s robotics models?
items.object: Early applications and deployment of Physical Intelligence’s robotics models
items.answer:
As a company, we're really focused on the long-term problem, and not any one particular application, because of the failure modes that can come up when you focus on one application. I don't know where the first applications will be. One thing that's actually challenging is that typically in machine learning, a lot of the successful applications, like recommender systems, language models, image detection, have humans consuming the model outputs who could check them. The humans are good at the thing.

A lot of the very natural applications of robots are actually the robot doing something autonomously on its own, where it's not like a human consuming the commanded arm position and then checking and validating it. I think we need to think about new ways of having some kind of tolerance for mistakes, or scenarios where that's fine, or scenarios where humans and robots can work together. That's one big challenge that will come up when trying to deploy these, and some of the language interaction work we've been doing is motivated by this challenge.

items.question: How do you assess humanoid robots as a form factor given the need to collect robot training data?
items.object: Humanoid robots and data collection
items.answer:
On one hand, humanoids are really cool, and I have one in my lab at Stanford. On the other hand, I think that they're a little overrated. One way to practically look at it is that I think we're generally fairly bottlenecked on data right now. Some people argue that with humanoids you can maybe collect data more easily because it matches the human form factor, so maybe it'd be easier to mimic humans. I've heard people make those arguments, but if you've ever actually tried to teleoperate a humanoid, it's a lot harder to teleoperate than a static manipulator or a mobile manipulator with wheels.

Optimizing for being able to collect data is very important, because if we can get to the point where we have more data than we could ever want, then it just comes down to research, compute, and evaluations. That's one of the things we're optimizing for. We're using cheap robots, robots that we can very easily develop teleoperation interfaces for, where you can do teleoperation very quickly and collect diverse data, collect lots of data.

items.question: How do you see embodied or physical intelligence fitting into intelligence more broadly?
items.object: Embodied or physical intelligence
items.answer: I feel like actually people underestimate how much intelligence goes into motor control. Many, many years of evolution led to us being able to use our hands the way that we do, and there are many animals that can't do it, even though they had so many years of evolution. I think there's so much complexity and intelligence that goes into being able to do something as basic as make a bowl of cereal or pour a glass of water. In some ways, I think that embodied intelligence or physical intelligence is very core to intelligence, and maybe kind of underrated compared to some of the less embodied models.

items.question: Which research developments do you see as turning points that made robotics feel like it was progressing faster?
items.object: Research turning points in robot learning
items.answer:
For us, there were a few things that we felt like were turning points, where it felt like the field was moving a lot faster compared to where it was before. One was the SayCan work, where we found that you can plan with language models as the high-level part and then plug that in with a low-level model to get a model to do long-horizon tasks. One was the RT-2 work, which showed that you could plug in a lot of the web data to get better generalization on robots.

A third was our RT-X work, where we were able to train models across robot embodiments. We basically took all the robot data that different research labs had; it was a huge effort to aggregate that into a common format and train on it. When we trained on that, we found that we could take a checkpoint, send that model checkpoint to another lab halfway across the country, and the grad student at that lab could run it on the robot. More often than not, it would do better than the model they had specifically iterated on themselves in their own lab. That was another big sign that this stuff is starting to work, and that you can get benefits by pooling data across different robots.

I think the ALOHA work and later the Mobile ALOHA work showed that you can teleoperate and train models on pretty complicated dexterous manipulation tasks. We also had a follow-up paper with the shoelace tying.

A third was our RT-X work, where we were able to train models across robot embodiments. items.question: Why did you build H-Robot as a hierarchical, interactive robot system?
items.object: H-Robot's hierarchical, interactive design
items.answer:
This was a really fun project. There's two things that we're trying to look at here. One is that if you need to do a longer-horizon task, meaning a task that might take minutes to do, then if you just train a single policy to output actions based on images—for example, if you're trying to make a sandwich and you train a policy that's just outputting the next motor command—that might not do as well as something that's actually thinking through the steps to accomplish that task. That was the first component; that's where the hierarchy comes in.

The second component is that a lot of the times when we train robot policies, we're just taking our data, annotating it, and saying, this is picking up the sponge, this is putting the bowl in the bin, this segment is folding the shirt. Then you get a policy that can follow those basic commands, like fold the shirt or pick up the cup. But at the end of the day, we don't want robots just to be able to do that. We want them to interact with us, where we can say, “Oh, I'm a vegetarian. Can you make me a sandwich? And I'm allergic to pickles, so maybe don't include those.” Maybe we can also interject in the middle and say, “Hold off on the tomatoes,” or something. It's a big gap between something that can just follow an instruction like “pick up the cup” and something that can handle those kinds of prompts and situated corrections.

We developed a system that has one model that takes the prompt as input and reasons through it, able to output the next step that the robot should follow. That might tell it the next thing will be “pick up the tomato,” for example. Then a lower-level model takes “pick up the tomato” as input and outputs the sequence of motor commands for the next half second. That's the gist of it. It was a lot of fun because we got the robot to make a vegetarian sandwich or a ham and cheese sandwich or whatever. We also did a grocery shopping example and a table-cleaning example.

items.question: How do you assess the value of vision versus tactile sensing for your robots?
items.object: Vision and tactile sensing in robots
items.answer: We've gotten very far just with vision, with RGB images. We typically will have one or multiple external, what we call base, cameras looking at the scene, and also cameras mounted to each of the wrists of the robot. I would love if we could give our robots skin. Unfortunately, a lot of the tactile sensors that are out there are either far less robust than skin, far more expensive, or very low resolution. There are a lot of challenges on the hardware side there. We've found that mounting RGB cameras to the wrists ends up being very helpful and probably gives you a lot of the same information tactile sensors can give you.

items.question: Why would you prioritize adding memory to your robot models over adding more sensors?
items.object: Prioritizing memory, data, and architectures over additional robot sensors
items.answer: For us, it's currently not a priority to look into these sensors because we think the bottleneck right now is elsewhere, on the data front and on the architectures. The other thing I'll mention is that most of our policies right now do not have any memory. They only look at the current image frame; they can't remember even half a second prior. I would much rather add memory to our models before we add other sensors. We can have commercially viable robots for a number of applications without other sensors.

items.question: How do you compare the challenges of making robotics commercially viable with those of self-driving?
items.object: Commercial robotics compared with self-driving
items.answer: Some parts of robotics make it easier than self-driving, and some parts make it harder. On one hand, it's harder because it's a much higher-dimensional space. Even our static robots have 14 dimensions, seven for each arm. You need to be more precise in many scenarios than driving. We also don't have as much data right off the bat. On the other hand, with driving I feel like you need to solve the entire distribution to have anything viable. You have to be able to handle an intersection at any time of day, with any possible pedestrian scenario or other cars. In robotics, I think there are lots of commercial use cases where you don't have to handle this whole huge distribution, and you also don't have as much of a safety risk. That makes me optimistic.

items.question: How do you think about whether the technology is ready for robotics companies to succeed today?
items.object: The timing of robotics and self-driving development
items.answer: A year ago, it would be completely different, and we've had so many new players recently. I think the fact that self-driving was like that suggested that it might have been a bit too early 10 years ago. I think deep learning has come a long way since then, and that's also part of it. With robotics, if you were to ask me 10 years ago or even five years ago, honestly, I think it would be too early. The technology wasn't there yet. We might still be too early, for all we know. It's a very hard problem, and how hard self-driving has been is a testament to how hard it is to build intelligence in the physical world.

items.question: How do you assess the advantages of robotics startups relative to large incumbent companies?
items.object: Robotics startups versus large incumbent companies
items.answer: In terms of major players, there are a lot of things I've really liked about the startup environment and a lot of things that were very hard to do when I was at Google. Google is an amazing place in many ways, but, as one example, taking a robot off campus was almost a non-starter for code security reasons. If you want to collect diverse data, taking robots off campus is valuable. You can move a lot faster when you're a smaller company, without the restrictions and red tape of the really big companies. They have a ton of capital and can last longer, but I also think they're going to move slower.

items.question: What would you prioritize if you were starting a robotics company today?
items.object: Starting a robotics company
items.answer: I think the main advice I would give someone trying to start a company would be to try to learn as much as possible quickly. I think trying to deploy quickly, learn, and iterate quickly—that's probably the main advice. Actually get the robots out there and learn from that. I'm also not sure if I'm the best person to be giving startup advice, because I've only been an entrepreneur myself for 11 months, but that's probably the advice I'd give.

items.question: How do you think about the value of observational data of people for training robotic models?
items.object: Observational data of people for training robotic models
items.answer:
I think that data can have a lot of value, but by itself it won't get you very far. I think there are some really nice analogies you can make. For example, if you watch an Olympic swimmer race, even if you have their strength, just their practice at moving their own muscles to accomplish what they're accomplishing is essential for being able to do it. Or if you're trying to learn how to hit a tennis ball, you won't be able to learn it by watching the pros.

Maybe these examples seem a little bit contrived because they're talking about experts. The reason why I make those analogies is that we humans are experts at low-level motor control already for a variety of things, and our robots are not. I think the robots need experience from their own body in order to learn. I think it's really promising to leverage that form of data, especially to expand on the robot's own experience, but it's really going to be essential to have data from the robot itself too.

items.question: How do you think about the kinds of experience that will matter for training robots?
items.object: Collected and autonomous experience for training robots
items.answer: When we collect data, it's kind of like puppeteering, like the ALOHA work. You can record both the actual motor commands and the sensor, the camera images, and so that is the experience for the robot. I also think that autonomous experience will play a huge role, just like we've seen in language models. After you get an initial language model, if you can use reinforcement learning to have the language model bootstrap on its own experience, that's extremely valuable.

items.question: How do you assess the breadth of experience that enables a robot to generalize?
items.object: Breadth of robot experience as a basis for generalization
items.answer: I think it all comes down to the breadth of the distribution. It's really hard to quantify or measure how broad the robot's own experiences are, and there's no way to categorize the breadth of the tasks—how different one task is from another, how different one kitchen is from another, that sort of thing. But we can at least get a rough idea of that breadth by looking at things like the number of buildings or the number of scenes, those sorts of things.

items.question: How do you envision the range of robot form factors that might emerge as robotic intelligence develops?
items.object: The future diversity of robot hardware and form factors
items.answer:
I don't know exactly, but I think my bet would be on something where there's a really wide range of different robot platforms. Sergey, my co-founder, likes to call it a Cambrian explosion of different robot hardware types and so forth, once we actually have the intelligence that can power all those different robots.

I think it's kind of similar to how we have all these different devices in our kitchen that can do all these different things for us, rather than just one device that cooks the whole meal. I think we can envision a world where there's one kind of robot arm that does things in the kitchen, with hardware optimized for that and maybe also optimized to be cheap for that particular use case, and another hardware type designed for folding clothes, dishwashing, those sorts of things. This is all speculation, of course, but I think a world like that is possible.
